turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Um... I guess I came in because... well, lately I just keep thinking it would be better if I didn't wake up. Just, you know, go to sleep and that's it. Sometimes I feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family and my crew. 

We do flooring, mostly tile and carpet, and my crew... we were supposed to finish this massive commercial tiling job over at the new strip mall. Have you seen it? The one with the huge parking lot. The grout we were using was this new epoxy kind, supposed to be totally stain-resistant, but it sets up so fast if the humidity is wrong. You really have to watch the humidity, but it's like nobody pays attention, and then you're on your knees for ten hours scraping it out with a hand tool. My knees are completely shot from it, honestly. I actually took some classes at the community college a while back thinking I'd get out of the trades, maybe do something at a desk where it's air-conditioned, but... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh. Yeah, I just... I just feel like I deserve the punishment. So they told me I had to come see you.

turns.doctor_question: Have you felt this way for most of the last two years, or is this a shift from how you were feeling a few months ago?
turns.patient_response:
Um, let's see... a shift? No, it's been... it's been about a year and two months now. It started a few months after my husband's injury. He hurt his back, actually. We were trying to move this incredibly heavy roll of commercial-grade carpet—the kind with the rubber backing that weighs a ton, you know? We had to get it up a flight of stairs because the freight elevator was broken at this office building we were working on. I told the general contractor we should wait, but he was breathing down our necks about the deadline. So my husband just tried to muscle it, and... pop. Just like that. 

The doctors said it was a herniated disc, L4-L5, I think? He was in a brace for months, couldn't even bend over to tie his shoes, let alone lay tile. I had to take over running the crew completely, which meant dealing with the suppliers directly, and they always try to short you on the underlayment if you aren't watching them like a hawk. I ordered 500 square feet of the good cork underlayment once, and they sent this cheap foam garbage that compresses to nothing in a year. 

But yeah, the... this heavy feeling, the depression... it really settled in a few months after he got hurt. About a year and two months ago, like I said.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly mentions experiencing a 'heavy feeling' and 'depression'.
symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient links the onset of their depressive symptoms to an identifiable stressor, specifically their husband's severe back injury.

turns.doctor_question: During the last fourteen months, have there been any periods of two months or longer where you felt completely like your usual self, without this heavy, depressed mood?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't. Honestly, for most of the time since this started... the guilt, the exhaustion, just not caring about anything anymore, and those thoughts about dying... they've just been there. I mean, some weeks are less crushing than others, but it never really goes away. It's like this thick dust that settles on everything. 

Speaking of dust, you wouldn't believe the amount of particulate matter we breathe in when we're pulling up old ceramic tile. Even with the N95 masks, which honestly, half the guys won't wear right anyway because they say it fogs up their safety glasses. My husband used to be so strict about the PPE, but after he hurt his back, the new guys I had to hire? Total cowboys. One of them, Jimmy, he decided to use a grinder on a concrete subfloor without sealing off the HVAC vents first. The dust got sucked right into the system and coated the entire first floor of this lady's house. It was a nightmare. I spent three days paying a professional cleaning crew out of my own pocket to fix it. 

But no, to answer your question... there hasn't been a break. Not for two months, not even close. It's just been this constant weight.

turns.doctor_question: During these past fourteen months, have there been any two-week periods where you experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in almost all of your usual activities, such as hobbies, work, or social life?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, um... absolutely. I mean, it's not even just a two-week period, it's been pretty much the whole time. I used to do so much. I used to paint, you know, watercolors mostly. And I'd cook these massive Sunday dinners for the family and the crew, and I even used to run three miles every morning before we'd start a job. I was also in this community theater group, showing up for rehearsals twice a week. 

But now... I don't know, all of those things just feel like chores. Like they belong to somebody else's life, not mine. I just don't care if I miss them anymore. 

It's funny I mentioned the theater group, because we were actually doing a production of Our Town right before my husband's accident. I was supposed to be Mrs. Webb. We had this set builder, Frank, who was completely obsessed with making the stage floor look like real dirt, but he didn't want to use actual dirt because of the mess. So he asked me to help him figure out a way to texture and paint plywood to look like hard-packed earth. We ended up using this mixture of joint compound and coffee grounds, actually. It looked amazing under the stage lights, but the smell... oh my gosh, the entire auditorium smelled like a stale espresso for a month. Frank was so proud of it though. He wanted to patent the technique. I wonder whatever happened to Frank... he moved to Florida, I think? Or maybe it was Arizona. Somewhere hot. 

But yeah, I just... I don't care about the painting or the cooking or any of it anymore. It just takes too much energy.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient mentions that doing her previous activities 'just takes too much energy,' indicating a loss of energy.

turns.doctor_question: During these past fourteen months, have you experienced at least five of the following symptoms at the same time: significant changes in your appetite or weight, sleeping too much or too little, feeling physically restless or slowed down, having very low energy, feeling worthless or excessively guilty, difficulty concentrating, or those thoughts about dying?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I definitely have a lot of those. The guilt, like I said, and the energy... I have zero energy. And my appetite is just gone. Most days I completely forget to eat until it's really late, or I'll just take a few bites of something and I immediately feel sick to my stomach. I've noticed my work pants have gotten really loose on me, and I'm definitely not trying to lose weight. 

It's actually a real problem with the work pants, because when you're kneeling on tile all day, if your pants are too baggy, the knee pads slide around. I buy these specific Carhartt double-front dungarees, they're the only ones that hold up to the thinset mortar. If you get thinset on regular denim, it basically turns to stone and then cracks the fabric when it dries. But these Carhartts, they're tough. My husband used to tease me because I'd buy them in this weird olive green color instead of the standard tan. He said I looked like I was going on a safari instead of laying porcelain. He always wore the tan ones. He had this one pair that was so covered in different colors of grout it looked like a camouflage pattern. I actually tried to wash them once with this heavy-duty citrus degreaser, and it completely stripped the color out of the fabric. He was so mad at me. 

But yeah, the pants are falling off me now. And the sleeping is bad too, and just feeling slowed down, like I'm moving through wet concrete. So yeah, definitely more than five of those things.
